paras: The Macon Western Union messenger strike was a walkout by white telegraph messenger boys at Macon, Georgia, in early January 1903, after which the company hired Black messengers in their place and the strikers threatened to mob them. No attack was reported, but several hundred of the company's patrons petitioned for the Black messengers' discharge.

The strike followed a cut in messengers' pay at the Western Union office from 2 cents to 1½ cents per message delivered. Manager Jackson argued that the boys could make up the loss by carrying packages, since the District Messenger Service now employed them and handled delivery for the company.

According to a Macon dispatch of January 2, ten boys had struck the night before, three had returned, and six remained out, leaving seven to do the office's work. The strikers abused the boys still working and threatened them with violence, and Jackson drove them from the back door by threatening to call the police. He also said that if he could not get enough white boys he would hire "negroes to deliver telegrams."

By January 3 the remaining white messengers had quit, and within a few hours fourteen Black messengers had taken their places. The white boys organized a union, said they would not return without their old wages, and, in the correspondent's words, declared "that they will mob the negroes."

Macon business men said employing Black messengers would hurt the company's patronage, and on January 5 a petition signed by several hundred of its principal patrons asked that the Black messengers be discharged and the white boys reinstated. The petition went to Superintendent B. F. Dillon at Jacksonville, while Assistant Superintendent Maxwell came from Savannah and said the office had hired Black messengers only "under compulsion" to keep delivering telegrams. No report of the petition's result, of any assault on the Black messengers, or of the strike's end appears in the coverage.

The episode is known only from three short Macon dispatches in the Savannah Morning News, headed "Messenger Boys Strike," "Western Union Puts in Negroes at Macon," and "Macon Men Petition for Messengers"; no Black-press coverage was found. The paper reported the threat to mob the replacements in a single sentence without comment and gave more space to the company's explanations and the patrons' objections.

accounts.label: Macon correspondent
accounts.gist: White messengers struck over a pay cut; the company replaced them with fourteen negroes, and the white boys organized a union and declared they would mob the newcomers.

accounts.label: Company officials
accounts.gist: Manager Jackson and Asst. Supt. Maxwell said the boys could make up the cut through package delivery and that negroes were hired only under compulsion to keep telegrams moving.

accounts.label: Macon patrons
accounts.gist: Business men and several hundred patrons objected to the Black messengers and petitioned for the white boys' return.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News ran brief Macon dispatches headed "Messenger Boys Strike" and "Western Union Puts in Negroes at Macon," reporting the mob threat in one sentence without comment and giving space to the company's and patrons' positions.

versions.value: Ten struck the night before Jan. 2, three returned, six were out on Jan. 2 with seven still working
All but three refused to work after being told of the cut, and those three quit on the morning of Jan. 3

conflicts.note: The later dispatch (A2) describes the walkout as complete by Jan. 3; the counts differ but the core event is the same.

set_aside: Separate brief strike of Western Union messengers at Savannah over the same pay cut; Macon mentioned only as having the same schedule.
News briefs judged by research to contain nothing on the Macon dispute; not reopened.
